lantern_10_001.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_001.text: Day 1502's first survey route followed the same closed footbridge path Yue had walked before the failed approach. Liao sent her with a local road worker named Ke Tan, who knew which private gates had permitted public passage and which had never done so. Yue carried the light paper bag allowed by her ordinary clearance. Ke carried the tools for the responsible crew's inspection. They were not interchangeable workers with interchangeable authority. Their shared task was to describe a route people could actually take, then check the proposed directions before posting them.

lantern_10_002.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_002.text: The first disputed gate belonged to a gardener, Wei Song, whose family had let neighbors cross an orchard for years. The bank closure now sent many strangers through it, including loaded animals that damaged the narrow path. Wei had closed the gate and left a note. The road office's older sketch showed the shortcut without naming the permission. Yue could see why pedestrians thought the gate had become a public road. Ke asked Wei to describe the earlier arrangement before anyone marked the closure as an unlawful obstruction.

lantern_10_003.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_003.text: Wei had allowed neighbors on foot during daylight and asked that the latch be closed behind them. She had never promised an indefinite cart route. The survey recorded that limited history and the current refusal. Ke knew a longer public lane, but its turn was difficult to see from the bridge approach. Yue proposed adding that turn to the new directional sheet. Wei offered a narrow foot passage for the next seven days while the sign was made, provided no animals entered. The road office accepted the temporary permission as temporary.

lantern_10_004.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_004.text: On the first afternoon Yue walked only the scheduled distance, returned to eat, and left the copying page until morning. She wanted to demonstrate that she could do the entire ordinary job effortlessly. Her clearance was for the arranged work, not for a performance of effortlessness. Ke had complained about blisters after his own route, and Liao had shortened the next day's standing discussion accordingly. These adaptations were part of getting the survey received. They did not require workers to turn every ordinary body limitation into a secret personal failure.

lantern_10_005.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_005.text: The clinic review on Day 1505 followed several days of normal light carrying and walking, with no recurrence of the provoking wrist sensation. Su observed the relevant ordinary movements, compared strength and sensation, and found no localized pain, tingling, or weakness. Yue had slept and eaten normally rather than testing her hand with extra loads. Su documented recovery from the recent symptom under those observed conditions. The assessment did not retroactively make Day 1491 normal or turn the failed preparation into a qualifying circuit. Both earlier findings remained in their dated records.

lantern_exam_recovery.speaker: narrator
lantern_exam_recovery.text: Shao received the qualified recovery report and Yue's actual work schedule. On Day 1506 she approved a return to reduced, dry route preparation first, with a later bounded live appointment considered separately after ordinary response. Yue's recovery was real; it was not an increased throughput ceiling or a stage-nine certificate. The failed approach's delayed stop remained the specific behavior to address. She could now plan new instruction from recovered conditions instead of continuing the old attempt. The paid clinical assessment and the restriction's end had actual dates, not a promise supplied by determination.

lantern_10_007.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_007.text: Yue expected relief to feel expansive. Instead it made her conscious of the next bill. The clinic's final review cost four copper, and a new yard block would require its own teaching and reference stock. Her survey contract would pay on received route batches, not all one hundred twelve before the first walk. She had room and food expenses through its end. Recovery had returned an opportunity to choose, not erased the cost of using it. She sat with the purse she actually possessed and postponed buying a fresh course until the first batch was accepted.

lantern_10_008.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_008.text: The temporary orchard passage produced its first disagreement the next morning. A man led a mule toward the narrow gate and argued that permission to pass meant permission to carry his goods in the easiest way. Wei pointed to the actual condition and refused entry. He accused the survey of favoring household comfort over trade. Ke offered the public lane and walked him to its turn. Yue recorded the incident because the proposed sign needed the animal route visible sooner. She did not ask Wei to surrender her garden merely to make their temporary arrangement look harmonious.

lantern_10_009.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_009.text: By the third day the gate's permission worked better for walkers and remained useless to carts, exactly as stated. The longer lane acquired its new direction board before the seven-day interval ended. Wei declined to renew the shortcut. Several neighbors were disappointed; one offered to pay for a more durable path. She did not want a busier passage beside her kitchen and said so. The office's public route remained available. Yue watched the gate close on its agreed final evening and removed the temporary arrow rather than leaving a convenient false promise nailed to a post.

lantern_10_010.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_010.text: A school parent, Wen Li, protested that the longer lane would make her daughter late. The school's timetable assumed the old bridge remained usable, although the bridge had been closed before term began. He Pu arranged a temporary later start for the affected group, then proposed a reviewed timetable for the next term. A change in a sign could reveal a conflict without solving it alone. Yue brought the actual walking distances to the meeting. Parents disagreed over whether children should walk in a supervised group or leave earlier from separate houses.

lantern_10_011.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_011.text: Wen Li preferred a supervised group and offered one morning each week. Another parent worked before dawn and could offer no mornings, though he could contribute a small agreed payment toward a paid escort. They did not treat those different contributions as proof of who cared more. The school found a local escort for the uncovered dates under a finite six-week arrangement funded by the parents who accepted it. Families that declined used their own route plans. The school notice named the particular received service, not a universal guarantee that every child had safely arrived.

lantern_10_012.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_012.text: Yue's first accepted survey batch covered two approaches and their checked directions. Liao paid thirty-two copper, eight calendar days of the contracted twenty-eight. The payment belonged to received ordinary work through Day 1509. Yue set aside the next room bill and spent six copper on a limited dry instruction block, three appointments with Shao on Days 1510, 1514, and 1518. No live cell came with that fee. She could afford the instruction presently and still needed the route wages for living. A new powered course would wait for an accepted, priced plan.

lantern_10_013.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_013.text: At the first dry appointment she described the moment of uncertainty that had preceded the delayed stop. Shao moved a marker while she spoke, and she practiced ceasing the hypothetical input before explaining its meaning. She found the sequence insulting until she moved the marker at a different point and she began interpreting it first again. The exercise had no actual charge to injure her wrist. Its point was to make the decision available before the next live temptation. A persuasive account afterward was a poor substitute for a stop at the time.

lantern_10_014.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_014.text: Shao asked what she would lose by stopping. Yue said the prepared route's completion, the appointment, and perhaps another cell. She asked what continuing uncertainly might lose. She named recovery time, the next job, and ordinary use of her hand. None of those quantities could be traded by adding more concentration to an account. The comparison did not mean she should never begin. It meant the actual start conditions and actual stop conditions needed equal force when the desired ending was close enough to seem already hers.

lantern_10_015.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_015.text: Afterward she helped Ke inspect a route beside the dye shop. The temporary roof repair had held in the first rain, but water from a blocked gutter ran across the walkway. The roofer's injury had not caused the blockage; the gutter cleaning had been omitted from an older separate job. Ke called the responsible property steward, who wanted the office to erect a warning board instead of paying to clear it. Liao accepted a temporary warning while the steward arranged the cleaning. She did not accept the board as a permanent replacement for ordinary maintenance.

lantern_10_016.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_016.text: The steward hired Lan De's helper for the cleaning at an agreed ordinary rate. Lan remained on restricted wrist work and was not made responsible for a ladder task because his name still appeared on an earlier roof receipt. Yue saw him sitting outside the clinic with a small book and stopped to talk. He missed being useful to his crew. His foreman had arranged a later light measuring job, but its date depended on assessment. Yue recognized the interval without claiming their injuries were equivalent. They compared the boredom of reading after one had stopped wanting to read.

lantern_10_017.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_017.text: That afternoon a storm arrived before the route crew reached its shelter. Yue and Ke waited in a pottery shed with permission from its owner, Rong De. He had lost one fired bowl in an earlier batch and refused Ke's joking suggestion that rainwater could fill the crack and make it valuable as a weather instrument. The bowl's intended use had been lost. A shard lay beside the shed's drain, doing a different small job. Rong let them stay until the rain eased, then asked for help moving empty crates within Yue's carrying limit.

lantern_10_018.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_018.text: They moved the light crates and left the heavy ones where Rong had arranged paid help for the evening. Ke wanted to do all of them to thank him for shelter. Yue asked whether the new job would delay their received survey inspection. It would, and the crates did not presently need rescuing from rain. They thanked Rong with the offered ordinary assistance and went back to their route. Gratitude could make an extra task desirable without making it compulsory or making its weight vanish. Ke admitted his shoulders were already tired.

lantern_10_019.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_019.text: In the inn, the wet afternoon had flooded Bai Yuan's small nursery yard. The cuttings on its lower bench were damaged, and the owner had moved those she could save before the water reached them. Yue asked whether there was a paid collection task suitable for her light work. Bai could pay for two hours sorting dry pots the following evening from her own remaining shop funds. Yue declined because it overlapped the survey's received meeting. Tian Rui took the accepted task after reading its demands. The nursery's need did not choose the available worker by friendship.

lantern_10_020.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_020.text: Bai lost most of the lowest tray. She did not call the surviving plants proof that the flood had benefited her shop. The lost tray had been a priced future sale and weeks of ordinary care. She offered replacements only to customers whose prepaid orders she could fulfill, refunding the others from the money set aside for those orders. Some buyers chose to wait for a later planting; others wanted their money back. Yue walked past the cleared yard and felt how much of town life involved honest endings too small to appear in any cultivation title.

lantern_10_021.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_021.text: The second dry appointment fell on Day 1514, after a shorter morning survey route. Yue rehearsed interruption during speech and during a deliberate ordinary step. Shao varied their order, then asked her to explain where each unfinished prepared segment would remain incomplete. She no longer needed to save the diagram's symmetry. She needed its marks to tell the next instructor what had actually happened. Her wrist remained ordinary under the dry activity. That was evidence for this reduced preparation's response, not a completed live great circuit or a reason to skip the later checks.

lantern_10_022.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_022.text: She took the ordinary following review on Day 1515 within the booked reduced block. Shao observed no renewed symptom and did not extend the appointment into a live test because the yard happened to be quiet. The relevant cell stock for her new work had not been purchased, and the qualified observer's current post belonged to another pupil. Yue went back to the survey with a clear afternoon plan. Having recovered did not make all later opportunities hers on demand. It made her able to accept them when conditions and a real booking aligned.

lantern_10_023.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_023.text: The fourth crossing approached a warehouse yard whose owner wanted pedestrians kept out entirely. The old map showed a public strip along its fence, but the fence had been moved during a repair. Ke measured against the road office's received boundary record, not against how long the new fence had looked established. The owner acknowledged the strip after the inspection and shifted stored crates away from it. Yue's directions could now name a permitted path without inviting walkers through the active loading area. The visible shortcut across the yard remained closed.

lantern_10_024.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_024.text: A warehouse worker complained that restoring the strip made him carry crates farther. The owner asked whether the road office would pay that labor. Liao declined; the extra arrangement followed the owner's obstruction of an existing passage, not a new requested service. The owner adjusted the crew's loading plan within their paid shifts. Yue had worried that clearing a path might merely move the inconvenience onto workers. Seeing the adjustment received by the crew mattered more than hearing the owner concede the boundary politely in an office where no one carried anything.

lantern_10_025.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_025.text: Ke pointed out a second old error: a direction sheet called the warehouse's southern door public because delivery clients had once used it. A client entrance and a public through-route had different conditions. Yue corrected the sheet after the property steward confirmed the actual admitted uses. Sun Luo wanted his shop described as a landmark and promised a discount if the printed route passed his sign. Liao would name a stable visible landmark where useful, but not move the direction to serve the offer. Yue declined the discount and bought her next thread at its ordinary price.

lantern_10_026.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_026.text: Sun was irritated, then helpful. His shop sign was visible from the actual route only in the morning because a delivery awning covered it later. He said so when Ke returned to check the directions in afternoon light. They chose a permanent wall mark instead. Yue thanked him for an observation that reduced his shop's role in the sheet. Sun shrugged. People arriving at the wrong turning would complain at his counter whether or not he received the advertisement. His interest in accurate directions was practical, with a little dignity mixed in.

lantern_10_027.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_027.text: The first sixteen received calendar days were paid by the second batch on Day 1517: another thirty-two copper, bringing Yue's survey wages received to sixty-four. Twelve days remained in the contracted term. Liao had accepted four checked crossing approaches and was waiting for two more. Yue did not call the remaining forty-eight copper a surplus available for a long examination series. The work had not yet been received, and living through the end of the term had costs. She planned a smaller possible next course instead of spending an attractive total before it existed.

lantern_10_028.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_028.text: Shao reviewed that proposal at the final dry appointment on Day 1518. Two later bounded live preparation sessions would cost eight in teaching and inspection plus four for two accepted reference cells, twelve in all, with ordinary following checks included. Their dates would depend on actual recovery and the survey schedule. Yue could fund that price from received money after setting aside the current room charge. She accepted the named plan, not an unlimited return to the failed route. The longer great-circuit examination still required a threshold she had not measured and work she had not completed.

lantern_10_029.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_029.text: The priced cells for those later sessions were ordered through the curriculum's separate stock. No association receiver window was shortened to fund Yue's practice. The association's existing fuel term remained its own received service through Day 1560, with its scheduled retirement assessment approaching. Hou brought a public invitation to that assessment and asked whether Yue intended to apply for a later documentary role. Three institutions were preparing different ordinary tasks related to the transition. Their offers had not yet closed. Yue asked for the actual terms rather than assuming the familiar desk would automatically be available again.

lantern_10_030.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_030.text: The first possible role was a public route account for the six-reach transition, based on admitted service information and new received ground checks. Its work would produce a public sheet but would not entitle its author to every private message carried by the old relay. The second was a maker's workshop record under a bounded license, paid better for a shorter private appendix and public safety page. The third concerned one local household's ordinary travel and care arrangement, paid from that household's accepted money and requiring no institutional endorsement. Their aims differed before any choice was made.

lantern_10_031.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_031.text: Yue took the offers home. Ma liked the public route work because residents needed to understand what changed after the tower's retirement. Rui liked the workshop offer because a maker could pay for concentrated technical writing without requiring the writer to justify every day before a public meeting. Tian asked about the household arrangement, whose fixed afternoons would leave more ordinary evenings free. None urged her to accept a vaguely superior life. They named things each knew from work, and Yue could hear the cost and attraction in every proposal.

lantern_10_032.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_032.text: Zheng Lin disliked the public route title because it made the old relay sound already dead. Hou corrected the title to distinguish the approaching retirement from the present three-window service, which continued with its paid accepted roster. Zheng appreciated that correction and still disliked the proposal. Bao asked whether he wanted his nephew to arrive before the last service day. He did. They wrote the ordinary travel booking together, accepting an arrival several days before the scheduled closure. A family visit could be arranged alongside institutional retirement without requiring either event to symbolize the other.

lantern_10_033.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_033.text: At the clinic Lan De's later assessment cleared a particular light measuring task, and the foreman booked him for it at a lower total wage than his former full work. Lan grumbled that the difference would hurt. His accident leave had covered its finite agreed period, not an indefinite equal income afterward. The crew discussed a paid supplement from its own welfare pot and accepted a bounded amount. Yue heard about it when the helper came to the inn. Ordinary care and ordinary income could both need attention, and neither problem solved the other automatically.

lantern_10_034.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_034.text: The survey's fifth crossing led past a shrine whose caretaker had placed benches across part of the public path for a festival. The festival itself was permitted under a local agreement, but the approved layout left a clear passage. Ke showed the caretaker the marked width. He moved the benches with two paid helpers from the festival's accepted budget, then asked whether Yue would attend the singing that evening. She would, if her remaining ordinary walking had not tired her. Rest could make a social invitation contingent without making the inviter feel rejected.

lantern_10_035.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_035.text: She went for the first part, sitting with Gao behind the lantern stalls. Gao had brought the library book he borrowed through his own card, and he kept it wrapped away from spilled tea. The singer forgot a verse and began another too soon. An older woman in the front supplied the missing line without seizing the whole song. Yue liked the brief negotiation: a voice faltered, another offered something specific, the first continued. Gao whispered that it was not an examination. Yue laughed and stopped trying to make the evening an illustration of her curriculum.

lantern_10_036.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_036.text: Their library date occurred the next afternoon. They read the interrupted-practice account separately and then argued about its language over tea. Gao thought the author sounded too pleased with stopping, as though any refusal were inherently wise. Yue pointed to the actual commenced activity and completed release. The author had begun the named work and stopped under its changed condition; the claim was narrower than Gao's first reading. Gao agreed about that passage and found another sentence he still disliked. Agreement on one observation did not turn them into readers with the same tastes.

lantern_10_037.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_037.text: On Day 1519, the following ordinary review after Yue's final dry appointment remained normal. Shao kept the first bounded live session booked for Day 1523, after another rest interval and appropriate current checks. Yue would not begin a full great circuit there. The course would test a changed interruption response within the old task, then observe the next day. She could describe that modest purpose without embarrassment now. Its smallness was what made the evidence useful. The route to a later title would pass through actual limited actions, not through an improving story alone.

lantern_10_038.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_038.text: The survey's last direction draft showed a school route that entered the public lane beside Wei Song's closed gate. Yue walked it with Wen Li and the paid escort, timing ordinary pace with stops rather than a brisk adult march. The group took longer than the first estimate. He Pu changed the arrival notice accordingly, and the parents decided whether their accepted arrangement still worked. Wei watched them pass from her kitchen. She no longer had strangers beside her door, and the children had a route whose duration included their real pace.

lantern_10_039.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_039.text: Wen Li admitted she missed the orchard shortcut. Wei admitted she missed seeing the neighbors who once passed quietly. Neither admission renewed permission to a crowd of carts and strangers. They agreed that Wen could visit for tea by invitation, which was a different relationship from public passage. Yue kept this invitation off the directional sheet. It belonged between the two women. The map improved by leaving a private friendship unprinted, even though the friendship helped make the loss of an old informal route feel less lonely.

lantern_10_040.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_040.text: A more uncomfortable invitation arrived on Day 1507, before the first survey batch was accepted. Yue's mother wanted to know whether an autumn visit was still possible. She had asked a neighbor to repair the room's leaking corner and would not promise to leave it empty indefinitely. A cousin needed lodging for a short apprenticeship in the district. Yue read the letter twice. Her mother's earlier welcome had been sincere, and her present request for a date was sincere too. Home was a place with other people's days inside it.

lantern_10_041.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_041.text: Yue drafted an answer saying she would come when the great circuit was finished. The phrase looked reasonable until she tried to attach a date. The certificate depended on measured conditions and recovered trials not yet achieved; the journey would take ordinary days and money even afterward. She tore up that draft. The next offered a possible later interval and asked whether it suited the household, while stating that it was not yet booked. Her mother could make her own room arrangement from an honest uncertainty instead of an elegant promise.

lantern_10_042.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_042.text: Tian Rui asked why Yue looked so unhappy over a letter containing no quarrel. Yue said she had imagined the room waiting exactly as she remembered it. Tian had returned to her own family's house once and found her old bed holding sacks of grain. They had moved the sacks for her visit, but she had first felt replaced. She laughed at the memory now and said the grain had probably fed her. Yue laughed too, not because the disappointment disappeared but because it acquired a familiar ordinary scale.

lantern_10_043.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_043.text: She sent the letter by the ground dispatch, paying its actual postage. The relay's institutional windows did not turn every resident's correspondence into instantaneous conversation. Her mother would receive it later and answer when she could. Meanwhile the cousin might accept another room or take the offered one. Yue had relinquished the comforting fiction that a household would suspend its needs around an unbooked return. She still wanted to go home. The desire could influence a later choice without becoming an obligation she imposed through a sentence in the present.

lantern_10_044.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_044.text: At the festival, Yan Di disappeared between the puppet stall and the singing circle. Ma was on a relief shift, and Lian had brought him with his mother's permission for the first songs. Lian thought the child had followed his mother to the food stalls; she thought he remained with Lian. Yue heard the two adults discover the misunderstanding near the shrine steps. The festival continued loudly around them. Neither wanted a speech about whose assumption was worse. They needed to establish where the child had last actually been seen.

lantern_10_045.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_045.text: Lian asked the stallholder while the mother checked the nearby benches. Yue stayed at the agreed meeting point with their bags, so Yan would find someone familiar if he returned. Ke told the festival steward, who organized a bounded ordinary search rather than inviting every stranger to pursue a vague description. A loud notice asked Yan to come to the shrine steps or speak to a named stallholder. It did not recite his household address or make an unverified claim that someone had taken him. The people responsible for him remained the people directing the search.

lantern_10_046.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_046.text: Yue could hear the singer carrying on through the notice. She wanted the whole festival to stop. The steward explained which people were searching and kept the path clear; emptying every stall would create another crowd with fewer fixed places for the child to recognize. Yue understood and still hated hearing applause. She held the elephant puppet that Yan had left in Lian's bag and resisted imagining it as the last object they would ever see. There was no evidence for that story, only the terrible ease with which fear could write it.

lantern_10_047.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_047.text: Han Tao's brother found Yan beside the old ferry stair. The child had followed another boy's paper bird and then waited at a landing that looked like the place from his mother's story. The current festival return boat used a different stair farther along the permitted path. Han brought him to the named stallholder, who sent word to the shrine steps. Yan had not been abducted, and the old landing had not secretly reopened. He had followed a remembered route without knowing that its ordinary receiving place had changed.

lantern_10_048.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_048.text: His mother held him tightly before asking what happened. Lian waited until she finished, then told Yan which meeting point they would use for the rest of the evening. The steward stood down the ordinary search and thanked its actual participants. Nobody announced that Yue had saved him by waiting in the assigned place. She had done one necessary small task among several. Her legs shook once the search ended. She sat with the bags while the family decided to leave early, their evening changed even though the child was physically unharmed.

lantern_10_049.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_049.text: The next day the adults wrote down the festival's actual meeting points and asked that future notices distinguish the old ferry stair from the current one. Yan's mother did not want his name printed in the public account, and the steward accepted a general description of the misunderstanding. Lian and she also changed their own handover words: each would say explicitly when the other had the child. The sign could help strangers; the words could help their particular family. Neither measure guaranteed that all future fear would be prevented by a sufficiently complete sheet.

lantern_10_050.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_050.text: Ma heard the story after her received shift and was furious with Lian for several minutes before listening to both accounts. Lian did not excuse the mistaken assumption by pointing at Ma's earlier broken dinner promise. Their household conflict and the child's festival confusion were different events with different people responsible. Yue was glad no one asked her to decide which sister had earned the right to be angrier. Ma called Yan's mother, heard the child's account, and helped choose a later ordinary outing. The lost evening did not need to become the family's final memory of the festival.

lantern_10_051.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_051.text: Yan asked whether the elephant could attend that later outing. Its new ears had bent in the bag while everyone searched. Pu could replace the little hinge strip but could not restore the old discarded head. Yan accepted the repair after specifying that the ears should still move separately. The materials cost a small actual sum that Lian paid, rather than disappearing inside Pu's hospitality. At the bench, Yan explained the paper bird he had followed. Pu listened without making the repaired puppet a reward for being lost.

lantern_10_052.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_052.text: Han Tao's brother felt guilty for having flown the bird where Yan could follow it. Han told him he had not been responsible for supervising another family's child. He had still helped bring Yan to the agreed stall once he recognized him. Both facts could be true without assigning him a debt for the whole search. Yue bought vegetables from Han afterward and thanked him for that actual help. He wanted to describe the patch's improved knot instead. She let the conversation move to what he had been trying to make all along.

lantern_10_053.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_053.text: The route survey added the changed ferry stair to its own received crossing approach. Ke checked the current landing's public access, and the boat keeper corrected a notice that used the old stair's local nickname for both places. He disliked losing the familiar name on the new sign. Wen Li pointed out that familiarity belonged mainly to adults who already knew where to go. The children needed a direction they could distinguish. They chose a new formal sign and kept the old nickname in conversation, where someone could ask which stair was meant.

lantern_10_054.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_054.text: At the school, the caretaker copied a simple route account into the reading lesson with the family's specific permission for an anonymous example. Yue declined to supply dramatic details from the bags she had watched. She had not seen those imagined events. He Pu used the actual mistaken meeting point and the actual fixed search location, then asked children how to clarify a handover. The lesson did not claim a paper exercise could replace adult attention at the next festival. It gave them words for a question they could ask before walking away.

lantern_10_055.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_055.text: Lan De attended the class because his light measuring job was at the school that morning. He said the children noticed the difference between two similar doors better than the adults who carried tools through them daily. Pu Mei asked whether that meant adults were bad at directions. He said adults sometimes stopped looking because a place felt known. Yue heard the answer from the doorway and thought of the elegant invented junction in her early route diagram. A familiar picture could hide a missing distinction until an actual task demanded it.

lantern_10_056.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_056.text: By the time Yue and Gao went to the library, the librarian had received three requests for the interrupted-practice account. He kept its ordinary loan period and offered another permitted public text while people waited. Yue did not get priority because her failure resembled the passage or because she had introduced the title to friends. Gao borrowed it through his own place in the queue. Waiting changed their planned tea date but did not cancel it. They went for tea first and returned on the date the book was actually available.

lantern_10_057.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_057.text: Their argument over the text became an argument over ambition. Gao thought Yue sometimes talked as though every ordinary job was a delay before her real life. Yue wanted to deny it and found evidence in her own phrases. She had called the survey a bridge to the next course, although people would use its directions after her course ended. Gao said earning money for training was a legitimate reason to work. It was not the only consequence of the work. Yue could admit the second without pretending the first had vanished.

lantern_10_058.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_058.text: Yue asked whether Gao never felt that way about the kiln. Gao said he did, especially when a bad firing consumed a week's effort. Then an apprentice would bring him a tile that fitted properly because of a measurement he had taught him. The kiln could be a livelihood, an irritation, and a place where his skill mattered beyond a future stage caption. Their tea cooled while they talked. Neither needed the other to surrender ambition in order to recognize a life already happening on the days before its hoped-for achievement.

lantern_10_059.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_059.text: On Day 1520 Yue paid twelve copper from received survey wages for two bounded live sessions before choosing. Her actual receipt covered instruction and reference stock; its appointment schedule remained separate from any later ordinary post she accepted. She made that distinction in her plan so an attractive employer could not seem to be buying her examination outcome. The employer would receive ordinary work of its own. Her later great-circuit qualification, if earned, would require its own evidence and funding. At present she had a recovered wrist and two modest sessions booked.

lantern_10_060.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_060.text: Shao reminded her that the reduced sequence was not a penitence. She wanted the new stop response practiced at a load already known to be bounded, so its actual following condition could be observed without adding an unprepared full route. Yue had begun calling the course a step backward. She asked backward from which completed ability. She had never completed the great circuit. Returning from a failed preparation to an appropriate actual task was a change in plan, not the loss of a certificate she secretly believed the money had bought.

lantern_10_061.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_061.text: The survey's public draft went on the notice board for corrections. Wei Song found the orchard permission described as current and pointed out that its seven days had ended. Yue had copied the temporary route annotation into the final draft by habit. She corrected it before printing and thanked Wei plainly. The mistake had not injured anyone because the draft was still open for received corrections. That did not make it harmless wording to retain. A completed ordinary review was doing the work it existed to do, with a particular error now removed.

lantern_10_062.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_062.text: Liao told Yue that public work often felt slower because readers could point at facts the author did not wish to revisit. A private workshop could have exacting review too, but its audience and retained information would differ. A household arrangement could be quieter and more intimate without being less binding. Yue looked at the three offers again that night. Their differences no longer felt like decorations over the same task. They would decide who could use her time, which papers could circulate, and whose disappointment she would encounter directly when a promise needed changing.

lantern_10_063.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_063.text: She slept before deciding, leaving the offers beside the ordinary oil lamp.

lantern_10_064.speaker: narrator
lantern_10_064.text: Day 1520 ended with Yue folding the three competing work offers beside the completed recovery record. The record was not a recommendation that she choose the noblest sounding job. It described an ordinary recovered body, reduced preparation, and later bounded appointments still ahead. The offers concerned where she would spend her time and which people could use the resulting work. She would have to choose soon. For that evening she cooked greens, listened to Tian's son practice a sentence from school, and let the future remain three actual possibilities rather than three promised rewards.
